title: "Exact binomial intervals"
execute:
  enabled: true

---

Normal intervals for a proportion can cross the boundaries of the parameter space, especially when successes are rare. The Hillenbrand paired vowel measurements produce such a case without invented counts.

The remaining question is how to obtain endpoints without relying on a normal approximation. We will turn each speaker's paired measurements into one binary response, invert two binomial tail tests, and then show why the same endpoints can be calculated as beta quantiles. That last step is an identity between two probability calculations; it does not change the interval into a Bayesian one.

This page reuses four earlier ideas. A [confidence interval](confidence-intervals.qmd) is a repeated-sampling procedure with random endpoints; [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) licenses the binomial count model for speaker-level Bernoulli outcomes; the success count $K$ is a [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd); and a [cumulative distribution function](../random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) gives each tail-event probability by accumulating probability up to a threshold.

## A within-speaker binary response

For each adult woman, define a success when /I/ in *hid* lasts longer than /i/ in *heed*. The speaker, not the vowel row, is the observational unit.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-binomial-data
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pairs_long <- subset(
  vowels,
  speaker_type == "woman" & vowel %in% c("I", "i"),
  select = c(speaker_id, vowel, duration_ms)
)
pairs <- reshape(pairs_long, idvar = "speaker_id", timevar = "vowel", direction = "wide")
names(pairs)[names(pairs) == "duration_ms.I"] <- "hid_ms"
names(pairs)[names(pairs) == "duration_ms.i"] <- "heed_ms"
pairs$hid_longer <- pairs$hid_ms > pairs$heed_ms

x <- sum(pairs$hid_longer)
n <- nrow(pairs)
p_hat <- x / n

stopifnot(n == 48L, x == 3L, !anyNA(pairs$hid_longer))
data.frame(speakers = n, successes = x, sample_proportion = p_hat)
```

The ordinary Wald interval is

$$
\widehat p\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{n}}.
$$

Here its lower endpoint falls below zero, which is impossible for a probability.

## Inverting binomial tail tests

Let

$$
X_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

and define the random success count

$$
K(\mathbf X)=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$

Then $K(\mathbf X)\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$. We use $K$ for this random count and $k=K(\mathbf x)$ for the count actually observed. Here $n=48$ and $k=3$.

The [confidence-interval page](confidence-intervals.qmd) defined random endpoints before observation. In the current case, the data enter through $K$, so write

$$
\left[p_{\mathrm L}(K),p_{\mathrm U}(K)\right].
$$

Once $K=k$ is observed, these endpoints become the numbers $p_{\mathrm L}(k)$ and $p_{\mathrm U}(k)$. The interval can fail in two ways:

$$
\left\{p<p_{\mathrm L}(K)\right\}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\left\{p>p_{\mathrm U}(K)\right\}.
$$

The Clopper--Pearson construction assigns at most $\alpha/2$ probability to each form of noncoverage. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}_p
\left(
p\notin[p_{\mathrm L}(K),p_{\mathrm U}(K)]
\right)
&\leq
\mathbb{P}_p\{p<p_{\mathrm L}(K)\}
+
\mathbb{P}_p\{p>p_{\mathrm U}(K)\}\\
&\leq \frac{\alpha}{2}+\frac{\alpha}{2}=\alpha.
\end{aligned}
$$

So the coverage is at least $1-\alpha$. We write “at least” because the binomial distribution is discrete: a nonrandomized rejection region generally cannot be chosen to have probability exactly $\alpha/2$ for every candidate $p$.

The remaining question is how to choose the endpoints. Consider a candidate value $p_0$ and suppose temporarily that $K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p_0)$. If $p_0$ is too small, observing $k$ or more successes is unlikely. Thus, for $k>0$, the lower endpoint is the boundary solving

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_{\mathrm L}(k)}(K\geq k)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
$$

If $p_0$ is too large, observing $k$ or fewer successes is unlikely. Thus, for $k<n$, the upper endpoint solves

$$
\mathbb{P}_{p_{\mathrm U}(k)}(K\leq k)=\frac{\alpha}{2}.
$$

This reversal is worth stating explicitly: the lower endpoint uses the **upper** binomial tail, while the upper endpoint uses the **lower** binomial tail. If $k=0$, set $p_{\mathrm L}(0)=0$; if $k=n$, set $p_{\mathrm U}(n)=1$.

## From binomial tails to beta quantiles

The binomial-tail identities are

$$
\mathbb{P}_p(K\geq k)=I_p(k,n-k+1)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}_p(K\leq k)=I_{1-p}(n-k,k+1),
$$

where $I_x(a,b)$ is the regularized incomplete beta function, or equivalently the CDF of a $\operatorname{Beta}(a,b)$ random variable evaluated at $x$.

The appearance of a continuous beta CDF inside a discrete binomial problem may initially seem strange. To see the connection, imagine placing $a+b-1$ points independently and uniformly on $[0,1]$. Let $Y_{(a)}$ be the position of the $a$th point from the left. This order statistic has the distribution

$$
Y_{(a)}\sim\operatorname{Beta}(a,b).
$$

Why do these parameters appear? For the $a$th point to lie near $x$, there must be $a-1$ points to its left and $b-1$ points to its right. Those two requirements supply the factors $x^{a-1}$ and $(1-x)^{b-1}$ in the beta density.

Now let $J$ count how many of the $a+b-1$ points fall at or below $x$. Each point independently has probability $x$ of doing so, and hence

$$
J\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(a+b-1,x).
$$

The event that the $a$th point falls at or below $x$ is exactly the event that at least $a$ points do so:

$$
\left\{Y_{(a)}\leq x\right\}
=
\left\{J\geq a\right\}.
$$

Thus the same probability has two representations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(x;a,b)
&=\mathbb{P}\left[Y_{(a)}\leq x\right]\\
&=\mathbb{P}[J\geq a]\\
&=\sum_{j=a}^{a+b-1}
{a+b-1\choose j}x^j(1-x)^{a+b-1-j}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This equality is not an approximation. The beta formulation tracks the position of an ordered point, while the binomial formulation counts the points at or below $x$. They describe the same event.

For the lower endpoint, set $a=k$ and $b=n-k+1$. Then $a+b-1=n$, so the beta CDF is the binomial upper tail $\mathbb{P}_p[K\geq k]$. For the upper endpoint, use the complement $\mathbb{P}_p[K\leq k]=1-\mathbb{P}_p[K\geq k+1]$. We can now solve the endpoint equations by taking beta quantiles:

$$
p_{\mathrm L}(k)
=F^{-1}_{\operatorname{Beta}(k,n-k+1)}(\alpha/2)
$$

for $k>0$, and

$$
p_{\mathrm U}(k)
=F^{-1}_{\operatorname{Beta}(k+1,n-k)}(1-\alpha/2)
$$

for $k<n$. The earlier [binomial definition](../random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd#definition) supplies the count model; the [beta definition](../random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd#definition) supplies the continuous CDF being inverted. This beta appearance is an algebraic identity, not a Bayesian posterior claim.

R's `binom.test()` performs the tail inversion. The equivalent endpoint code is `qbeta(alpha / 2, k, n - k + 1)` and `qbeta(1 - alpha / 2, k + 1, n - k)`, with the two boundary rules above.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-binomial-intervals
exact_result <- binom.test(x, n, conf.level = 0.95)
wald_se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
wald_interval <- p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * wald_se
exact_interval <- as.numeric(exact_result$conf.int)
beta_interval <- c(
  if (x == 0L) 0 else qbeta(0.025, x, n - x + 1L),
  if (x == n) 1 else qbeta(0.975, x + 1L, n - x)
)

intervals <- data.frame(
  method = c("Clopper-Pearson", "Wald"),
  estimate = p_hat,
  lower = c(exact_interval[1], wald_interval[1]),
  upper = c(exact_interval[2], wald_interval[2])
)
stopifnot(wald_interval[1] < 0)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(exact_interval, beta_interval, tolerance = 1e-12)))
intervals
```

The Clopper--Pearson exact binomial interval is [`r sprintf("%.4f", exact_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.4f", exact_interval[2])`], while the Wald interval is [`r sprintf("%.4f", wald_interval[1])`, `r sprintf("%.4f", wald_interval[2])`]. Here *exact* means that the stated coverage guarantee follows under the IID Bernoulli model; it does not remove that model assumption.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-binomial-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Intervals for the probability that /I/ lasts longer than /i/ within an adult woman."
ggplot(intervals, aes(estimate, method, xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, 1), color = "grey75", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.15, color = "grey35") +
  geom_point(color = "#8B1A1A", size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Speaker-level success probability", y = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

“Exact” means that the calculation uses the finite binomial distribution rather than a large-sample normal approximation. It does not make the common-probability assumption, speaker independence, or connection from this screened cohort to a broader population exact.

## Recap and forward link

1. $K$ is the random count; $k$ is the count observed in this sample.
2. The lower endpoint rejects candidate probabilities that make $K\geq k$ too rare, while the upper endpoint rejects candidates that make $K\leq k$ too rare.
3. Discreteness makes the procedure conservative: coverage is at least, and not generally exactly, $1-\alpha$.
4. Beta quantiles compute the same endpoints because binomial tails can be written as beta CDFs.

The [bootstrap page](bootstrap-confidence-intervals.qmd) next constructs an interval when no such exact finite-distribution inversion is available.

## Check your understanding

1. Why is the speaker the independent unit?
2. Which defect of the Wald interval is visible here?
3. What distribution is inverted by the Clopper--Pearson procedure?
4. Which assumptions remain even after using an exact calculation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Each success compares two vowels from the same woman, so the binary outcome belongs to the speaker rather than to either vowel row separately. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The Wald interval's lower endpoint falls below zero, outside the parameter space for a probability. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The procedure inverts finite binomial tail probabilities, equivalently using beta quantiles for its endpoints. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Even the exact Clopper--Pearson interval assumes independent speakers and a common success probability; generalization still depends on the screened cohort's recruitment. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
